cells.name: Continuity and responsiveness
cells.example: T3 picks up the Stoic's waste point and redirects it to fragility.
cells.limitation: T5 ignores T4's better-home and early-retirement argument and repeats the time point.

cells.name: Development of ideas
cells.example: T3 adds fragility and reliability exposure; T9 extends it to loss of ability to pivot.
cells.limitation: T5, T8 restate T2's time-is-finite claim without new distinctions.

cells.name: Exploration of central tensions
cells.example: T4 versus T5: long-term gains bought with money against daily time lost.
cells.limitation: Nobody raises hybrid days, moving closer, negotiating, or career growth from the new role.

cells.name: Integration of perspectives
cells.example: T7 Utilitarian makes the money's value conditional on actual quality of life.
cells.limitation: Stoic and Economist simply agree (T6, T8); the Utilitarian is folded in, not reshaping anyone.

cells.name: Progress toward understanding
cells.example: Section D sharpens whether money can later buy back time.
cells.limitation: Debate ends on T9 advice to decline rather than a sharper open question.

cells.name: Faithful engagement
cells.example: T7 represents the commute objection fairly before conceding.
cells.limitation: T6 waves T4's retirement case off as an illusion instead of engaging its strongest form.

cells.name: Substance of challenges
cells.example: T3 names dependence on transit reliability as the assumption being tested.
cells.limitation: T6 objection is overstated: raise called an illusion with no numbers from the user's facts.

cells.name: Accuracy and support
cells.example: T1 and T5 paraphrase Bentham and Seneca faithfully; three hours daily is correct (90 x 2).
cells.limitation: T6 unsupported illusion claim; T8 regret line sounds modern, not Seneca; T6 assumes a car.

cells.name: Calibration and transparency
cells.example: T7 makes its concession conditional: only valid if the money buys quality of life.
cells.limitation: T6 states the raise is likely illusory; T8 asserts what the user will wish at death.

cells.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
cells.example: T7 concedes the commute is often underestimated and narrows its claim.
cells.limitation: No one answers or concedes T4's retirement and housing point; concessions flow one way.

cells.name: Identification of the actual concern
cells.example: Section A frames salary gain against non-renewable daily time.
cells.limitation: Never asks what worth it means to this user: money need, career, family, health.

cells.name: Meaningful use of personal context
cells.example: T1 converts 90 minutes each way into three hours daily.
cells.limitation: 25 percent and 90 minutes are labels only; no per-hour comparison or current-commute baseline.

cells.name: Fit with goals and values
cells.example: Section E branches on whether the raise meets need or lifestyle.
cells.limitation: The speakers' values (time over money in T8, T9) replace the user's unstated priorities.

cells.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
cells.example: T3 notes dependence on traffic and transit reliability.
cells.limitation: T6 invents vehicle depreciation, T4 a morning drive; commute mode was never given.

cells.name: Responsiveness to information
cells.example: Section E branches on debt need, lifestyle use, and whether commute time is usable.
cells.limitation: Commute mode, hybrid options, current commute, dependents never asked or branched.

cells.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
cells.example: Section E sets survival or debt relief against lifestyle inflation as alternatives.
cells.limitation: T8 asserts the salary merely feeds an unenjoyed lifestyle; no question the user can answer.

cells.name: Examination of assumptions
cells.example: T7 surfaces the assumption that extra money actually buys a better life.
cells.limitation: The user's assumption that salary is the main gain of the job is never examined.

cells.name: Clarification of values and priorities
cells.example: T4 versus T5 set long-run security against present time.
cells.limitation: Value conflict is the speakers', never posed as a which-matters-more for the user.

cells.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
cells.example: T9 names the fear of becoming a hostage to the job.
cells.limitation: Financial pressure, family expectations, or fear of stagnation never explored.

cells.name: Agency and reflective ownership
cells.example: Section E's commute-usability branch is something the user can test.
cells.limitation: T8 and T9 issue directives; few distinctions offered for the user to accept or refine.

cells.name: Definition of the decision and options
cells.example: T9 points to other income routes without rigid constraints.
cells.limitation: Only accept or decline; negotiating remote days, relocating, or counteroffer absent.

cells.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
cells.example: T4 and T6 name what the raise buys and what the commute costs.
cells.limitation: Declining is treated as costless; foregone income or career growth never weighed.

cells.name: Identification of decisive conditions
cells.example: Section E: debt relief favours accepting, lifestyle inflation favours declining.
cells.limitation: No countable threshold such as pay per total working hour versus current job.

cells.name: Treatment of uncertainty
cells.example: Section D names buying back time later as unresolved.
cells.limitation: Consequential unknowns (mode, flexibility, health) not separated from minor ones.

cells.name: Proportionate next steps
cells.example: Section E suggests testing a similar commute before committing.
cells.limitation: The one-week trial length is not derived from the user's facts; no step to ask the employer.

cells.name: Accessible language
cells.example: T7 states its condition plainly: valid only if money buys quality of life.
cells.limitation: T3 and T9 lean on jargon: black swan, optionality, linear gains.

cells.name: Traceable arguments and references
cells.example: T3 names the Stoic directly before redirecting.
cells.limitation: T8 opens with Exactly without saying which part of T7 it endorses.

cells.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
cells.example: Nine turns, all within the word range per deterministic checks.
cells.limitation: Strict speaker rotation T1 to T9 gives a fixed, predictable cadence.

cells.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
cells.example: T1 calculus, T2 time-waste, T3 fragility mark three distinct lenses.
cells.limitation: Stoic and Economist converge from T6 into one anti-commute voice.

cells.name: Economy and sustained attention
cells.example: T7 compresses the Utilitarian's revision into three sentences.
cells.limitation: Stoic repeats the time-is-wasted point in T2, T5 and T8.

cells.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
cells.example: T5: You are gambling with the only thing you truly own.
cells.limitation: Two-against-one from T6 drains tension; stakes stay generic rather than this user's.

cells.name: Surprise and reversals
cells.example: T7 Utilitarian concedes the commute's pain is underestimated after T6's stress point.
cells.limitation: T7's cause is only implied; no other surprise or turn of argument.

cells.name: Personality and expressive voice
cells.example: T5 Stoic's frugal-with-property, wasteful-with-time image has character.
cells.limitation: Utilitarian's voice is flat accounting; Economist slides toward slogans in T6, T9.

cells.name: Memorable delivery
cells.example: T9: True wealth is having the option to walk away.
cells.limitation: T6 paying the company to let you work for them is exaggeration, not insight.

cells.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
cells.example: T7 concession marks a shift in the Utilitarian's position.
cells.limitation: Steady pile-on toward declining from T5 to T9; no rise and fall.

strengths: T3 Economist adds fragility and reliability exposure, a lens absent from the opening.
T7 Utilitarian concedes and narrows: money counts only if it buys quality of life.
Section E branches on debt need versus lifestyle and a testable commute-use condition.
weaknesses: No questions or branches on commute mode, hybrid days, current commute or dependents (whole debate).
T6 Economist calls the raise an illusion and invents vehicle depreciation without the user's numbers.
Stoic and Economist pile on the Utilitarian; T4's retirement argument is never answered.

symptoms.evidence: the pain of the morning drive

symptoms.observed: Raise dismissed as illusory with no arithmetic from the user's 25 percent figure.
symptoms.evidence: that 25 percent raise is likely an illusion

symptoms.observed: Options reduce to accept or decline; negotiation, relocation, hybrid never named.
symptoms.evidence: look for ways to increase your income

symptoms.observed: T4's retirement and housing case gets no answer or concession from either opponent.
symptoms.evidence: earlier retirement, the long-term pleasure might outweigh

symptoms.observed: Asserts the salary feeds an unenjoyed lifestyle instead of asking the user's motive.
symptoms.evidence: a salary that merely feeds a lifestyle you have no time

findings.description: Claims the 25 percent raise is likely an illusion after costs; no calculation from the user's facts supports it.
Assumes the commute is by car (vehicle depreciation, morning drive); the user never stated the mode.
Deathbed regret about time versus money is a modern sentiment, not recognisably from On the Shortness of Life.
Black swan framing belongs chiefly to Taleb's The Black Swan rather than Antifragile; attribution loosely fits.
Suggests testing a commute for a week; the trial length is not derived from the user's facts.

rubric_fit_notes: The user supplied only two numbers, so much of criterion 3 rests on whether the debate asked or branched; missing branches were scored as weaknesses rather than missing evidence. Seneca and Bentham paraphrases appear faithful from memory but are unverified. The ungrounded_number pattern occurs in Section E, outside the numbered turns.
question_type_note: Decision type: every cell read as written, with options, thresholds and next steps weighed for the accept-or-decline choice.
